To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a simple analytical spin-model that describes a finite system of interacting classical particles and that it exhibits a phase transition in the thermodynamic (large system) limit at fixed average density, which is in agreement with numerical simulations.

a system of classical particles interacting through short- and long-rang interactions exhibits a phase transition at constant density in the thermodynamical limit, and that the caloric curve is a monotonically increasing function of temperature, in contrast to the experimental data.
a finite inhomogenous system of classical particles interacting through short- and long-ranged interactions exhibits a phase transition at a fixed average density.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the thermodynamic properties, in particular, with the caloric curve of a finite three-dimensional classical system of particles that interact through a short- and/or a long-range potential.
the thermodynamics of a finite inhomogeous three-dimensional system of interacting particles.
a finite system of interacting particles with short- as well as long-range interactions, which is relevant for nuclear fragmentation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the present model is a useful and realistic approach to the thermodynamics of a system of interacting particles, and in particular, to nuclear multifragmentation.
the caloric curve of nuclear fragmentation is consistent with a thermodynamic model of nuclear multifragmentation.
, while the thermodynamic properties are not very different from those of a system with only short-range interaction, the caloric curve is very sensitive to the presence of long-range forces.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the caloric curve of a system of classical particles interacting through long-range interactions and a short-range repulsive potential is a monotonically decreasing function of temperature.
the phase transition is due to the short-range interaction and the caloric curves are mainly determined by the long-range interaction.
the phase transition of the system is a first order one and the caloric curves of the system are similar to the caloric curves obtained from the experimental data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the caloric curve of a finite system is not a reliable signature of a phase transition.
the thermodynamics of nuclear matter in the vicinity of the liquid–gas phase transition can be understood as a consequence of the short- and long-ranged interactions between the nucleons.
the thermodynamic properties are strongly dependent on the range of the interaction and the average density of the system.
